older and younger adults differ in the extent to which they use verbatim information to reject categorically related test items, and that the ability to do so is positively correlated with conceptual memory span and fluid intelligence in both older and young adults.
the capacity of older adults to adaptively and flexible use episodic memory is attenuated and that the capacity to do so is positively correlated with level of fluid ability.

older and younger adults were asked to make episodic decisions at different levels of item-specific versus category-based specificity, and that the likelihood that participants would reject categorically related items under item-specific instructions positively correlated with conceptual (i.e., semantic) span, level of fluid intelligence, and level of frontal functioning.

how aging affects the capacity of older and younger adults to flexibly use their episodic memory in a way that is sensitive to task demands.
the effects of aging on the ability to flexibly and adaptively use information in memory at different levels.
the role of episodic memory and executive function in the flexible use of knowledge.

the findings of the present study suggest that interventions that enhance the flexibility of episodic memory, and vice versa in older adults, may also improve the flexibility of cognitive functioning.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
older adults can be helped to think more flexibly by improving fluid intelligence, and this can help them remember better.

the flexibility of memory processes in older adults is not as strong as it is in younger adults, but that the two groups are similar in their ability to adapt to different types of memory instructions.
aging and fluid intelligence are related to the ability to flexibly remember.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ability to flexibly adapt to task demands is an important component of successful cognitive aging.
the ability to adaptively use episodic memory in a flexible way is not only a function of age but also of cognitive ability.
the flexibility of thinking is a key aspect of healthy cognitive aging, which is often overlooked in research.
